# Advice to Non-users

> "Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn't have another to lift him up."
>
> — Ecclesiastes 4:9-10

This chapter is for the people standing next to the man in the trap: his wife, his parents, his pastor, his friends. If that's you, and you've skipped straight here, welcome. Please go back and read the whole book afterwards. You can't help a man out of a trap you don't understand.

If you're the man himself, read on anyway. Some of this is for you, and the part on slipping is all for you.

## Getting him to read this book {-}

Begin by reading it yourself, and try to stand where he stands.

Don't push the book at him with a speech about what he's doing to his marriage, his mind or his soul. He knows. He has known for years, and he has preached himself that sermon more often and more harshly than you ever could.

Here is what's hard to grasp from outside. He doesn't keep doing it because he likes it. He may say he does, to you and to himself, because a man has to hold on to some dignity. He does it because he believes he can't manage without it. He thinks it calms him down, sends him to sleep and gets him through bad days. Underneath that sits a deeper dread: that life without it would be grey, and that a man who stops is only half a man.

So if you corner him, you get a cornered animal. Demand that he stop and he'll want it more. He'll also get better at hiding it, and a hidden habit grows more precious. Chapter 15 was about exactly that.

Work on the opposite side instead. Don't tell him how bad it is. Show him it can be left. If you're a man who has got out, say so. A single sentence from someone he respects, "That had me for fifteen years and it's gone," will do more than any lecture. If you're not, find him one: a book, a testimony, an older man at church with some sense. Be a little careful where you send him. Many of the forums run on streak counters and gritted teeth, which is the Willpower Method with a crowd watching.

Once he believes it's possible, his mind opens a crack. That's when you can pass on the one idea this whole book hangs on: the "relief" he gets is only the ending of an itch the habit itself created. It isn't relaxing him. It's the reason he's tense.

By then he may be willing to read. He'll be braced for two hundred pages of hellfire or hormone charts. Tell him there's neither. Tell him it doesn't even ask him to stop until the end.

And don't make it strange. Don't stage a confrontation, and don't try to win an argument. If you win it, you've lost him. Mention it once, plainly and kindly, and leave the book where he can find it.

For friends in particular: a man is helped by other men. One veteran pastor's advice to men fighting sexual sin: "Get in a group where you exhort one another every day against the deceitfulness of sin." You needn't form a committee. Two honest friends are a group. Just be sure the exhorting sounds like good news and not like a parole hearing.

## To the reader: should you tell her? {-}

Chapter 28 gave my answer, so I'll only add what belongs here.

She may already know, because you've been failing in front of her for years with streaks and promises. If so, tell her you've found a different way and hand her the book. A wife who understands the trap is worth ten who are merely worried about it.

If she doesn't know, and you're walking out happily, there's no rush to make an announcement for your own relief. Get free first. Then tell her in good time and for her sake, the way Chapter 28 described. She'll probably have noticed something already. Wives usually spot the change in a man before he mentions it.

If you're struggling, don't struggle alone behind a closed door. That's where the habit lived, and it's the worst place to fight it. Ask for help: hers, or a trusted man's.

## To wives {-}

Now to you directly.

First, this was never about you. He almost certainly brought the habit into the marriage from his teens. It isn't a verdict on your looks, your body or how often you say yes. Men married to women they adore are caught in it, and a single man is caught in just the same way. Do not pick up blame that isn't yours.

Wives nearly always pick it up anyway. One pastor's wife, writing about her husband's pornography, put the first question in six words: "Am I not enough for him?" She went on, "I felt ugly and unwanted." If that has been your question, the answer is that you were never the measure. The habit was there before he knew your name.

The same goes for the bedroom. If he has seemed far away there, or slow, or simply uninterested, Chapter 8 explained why: years of the habit train a man's body to answer to his own hand. They spend on nothing the desire that was meant for you. One young man on a forum wrote of the girl he loved, "She started to think it was her fault, but deep inside, I knew what the problem was." It wasn't her fault, and it isn't yours. A woman who had lived through it from the other side said the worst of it was the silence: "I was not told about it until late in the relationship." That is why Chapter 28 told him to tell you. In most men this mends once the habit has gone, though it can take weeks or months, and patience helps it more than pressure does.

Second, you're allowed to be hurt. Calling it a trap explains it. It doesn't excuse it, and it doesn't cancel what it cost you. He stopped in a day. Trust comes back more slowly, and that's normal.

Third, a warning. In some marriages the habit is one thread in something bigger: pornography, years of lying, anger turned on you, or worse. This book can't untangle that, and you shouldn't try to do it alone. Talk to a pastor you trust or a Christian counsellor. Getting help is not disloyalty.

Now, supposing he's stopping and you want to help, here is how.

**Assume the first weeks cost him something, whether they do or not.** Don't tell him it's easy. If it is easy he'll find that out for himself, and he'll enjoy telling you.

**Praise him, and keep it up.** Tell him you're proud of him. Tell him he looks better, that he's better company, that you like having him back. In the first few days he'll be carried along by the fresh start. That glow fades fast, and it's in week three that an encouraging word is worth most.

**Don't be afraid to mention it.** He may go quiet on the subject, and you may think he'd rather forget. Usually it's the opposite, especially if any willpower is involved. He's thinking about little else. Ask how he's doing. He'll soon say if he'd rather you didn't.

**Take some pressure off.** For a few weeks, go out of your way to make ordinary life pleasant. Plan something to look forward to. If he's short-tempered, try not to hit back, hard as that is. It's no small thing to ask of you, I know.

**Don't fall for the tantrum.** A man stopping by willpower sometimes plays a trick, often without knowing he's doing it. He makes himself so unbearable that someone finally says, "Oh, for heaven's sake, do whatever you need to do." Then he hasn't given in. He's been given permission. If he tries it, don't hand him the permission. Say, "If this is what that thing did to you, thank God you're nearly rid of it. I think you're brave."

**Don't become his policeman.** Don't check his phone, time his showers or ask for a nightly report. Chapter 28 told him not to turn you into a parole officer, and I'm telling you not to accept the job. A man who behaves because he's watched isn't free. He's supervised. You can't want his freedom into being, and you aren't responsible for it.

**Look after yourself.** Two people are recovering here. Keep your own friends, your own prayers, your own interests, and someone wise to talk to who isn't him.

One last thing about the bedroom. Don't try to compete with the habit or stand in for it. You're a person and can't be his substitute. Chapter 21 told him plainly that stopping doesn't mean holding back from you. The marriage bed is the opposite of the trap, because there are two of you in it.

## To parents {-}

Most men in the trap fell in as boys, alone, with nobody explaining anything. Several of the men quoted in this book started at ten. That's the age to think about, and it's earlier than you'd like.

Don't imagine the boys aren't looking for help, either. Under one video about beating lust, among thousands of comments from grown men, sits this one: "I'm fourteen and I need this. I have a future but I don't wanna ruin it." He was asking strangers on the internet because nobody at home had said a word.

James Dobson, whose soft line Chapter 4 argued with, was right about one thing. Writing to parents of teenagers about the danger of a boy becoming obsessed, he said: "I believe the best way to prevent that kind of obsessive response is for adults not to emphasize or condemn it."

He was right about *condemn*. Shame a boy and you teach him two things: that he's disgusting, and that he must hide better. You've then manufactured the secrecy and self-loathing that the habit feeds on. Paul's instruction fits: "You fathers, don't provoke your children to wrath, but nurture them in the discipline and instruction of the Lord."

But the alternative to condemning isn't silence. Silence is how you and I got here. The alternative is an explanation, given calmly, by someone who isn't shocked.

So, fathers, a few suggestions.

- **Speak before the world does.** One man who was caught at ten, and now talks about it publicly, tells parents to "be the first presenter of truth to your children." If you wait until you've "caught" him, you're already late. The conversation starts as a trial.
- **Tell him the truth about the trap.** Tell him desire is good and God-made. Tell him this habit hijacks it, that it promises relief and delivers an itch, and that nearly every man who starts wishes he hadn't. You've just read a whole book on the subject. Give him the ten-minute version.
- **Tell him your own story,** as much of it as is fitting. Nothing takes the shame out of a boy faster than finding out his father has been there and got out.
- **Never spy and then explode.** If you find something, wait a day. Then talk to him the way you wish someone had talked to you.
- **Use ordinary sense about screens.** I said fences don't free a man, and they don't. But a twelve-year-old with a private screen in his bedroom at midnight isn't being trusted. He's been abandoned to it. Keeping phones out of bedrooms at night is plain parenting, and it's a good rule for the adults as well.
- **When he's old enough, give him this book.** You're the judge of when.

If you're a mother raising a son without his father, you can say most of this yourself, and he'll survive the embarrassment. If you can't, find a man you trust, a grandfather or uncle or youth leader, and ask him to.

And if your son is already grown and already caught, everything in the first section applies. He's not a child to be managed. He's a man to be told that a way out exists.

## To pastors {-}

You know better than I do how many men in your congregation this touches. You also know how rarely the word is said aloud in church. Chapter 4 quoted the man who wrote that it is "not addressed in the pulpit at all". I'm asking you to say it.

Say it calmly and without drama. Don't make it the worst sin in the catalogue, which helps nobody. Don't give a nervous joke in the men's breakfast either, which helps even less. Say something like, "Many of you are caught in this, here is why, and here is the door." Men have sat under you for years believing they were the only one. One sentence from you ends that.

Three things, if I may.

**Keep it in proportion.** C.S. Lewis wrote: "The sins of the flesh are bad, but they are the least bad of all sins." He wasn't waving them through. His point was that the cold sins of the spirit, with pride first among them, are worse. A man who's been taught that this is the unforgivable one will hide it from you, and a man who is hiding can't be helped.

**Lead with hope.** Your men are already expert in guilt. Guilt is what sends them back, as Chapter 1 explained. The Canadian pastor Tim Challies ended a hard-hitting article on this subject with the sentence your men most need: "For those who struggle with this sin, take heart, for there is hope."

**Be careful with the usual tools.** Pledges, weekly check-ins, software and streak charts all share one assumption: that the man wants it and must be stopped. That's the Willpower Method baptised. Use what you judge wise. But aim past behaviour at belief. A man who no longer wants it doesn't need restraining.

If a man comes to you and confesses, remember what it cost him to knock on your door. Thank him first, and say whatever else you need to say after that.

## A note on women {-}

This book is addressed to men, but the trap doesn't check who walks in. As Chapter 4 said, pastors who write honestly about it reckon that nearly as many women as men have tried it. Read the comment threads on any Christian article about the habit and you'll find women's names all through them:

> "it feels like something is latched on to my soul and sucking the good out of it every time i masturbate."
>
> — a commenter on a Christian recovery blog

> "it makes me feel like crap, disgusted, and less worthy"
>
> — another commenter on the same blog

A woman of thirty-two, writing under a testimony video, described the same loop the men describe: "I would repent, be fine for a couple/few weeks, then BAM!" And the same damage: "The shame of it ... made me not want to pray or talk to God."

If you're a woman reading for yourself, everything here applies. The Little Monster is the same itch and the Big Monster tells the same lies, with one or two of its own added: "it's empowering", "it's self-care". Change the pronouns and read on.

The loneliness can be worse for you, since even churches that talk about this talk as though it were only a male problem. It isn't, and you aren't strange. The door out is the one men use.

## Slipping {-}

This section is a warning. I'm not giving you permission. I hope you never need it.

First, a word about words. The forums call it a "relapse" and reset the counter. We don't have a counter, as Chapter 28 said, and the word "relapse" does damage of its own. It turns one stupid act into an identity: *I'm a relapser.* What actually happened is smaller. You slipped, you fed the Little Monster, and the feeding woke the Big Monster, who is now telling you lies. Learn to recognise them.

- **"I'll never be free."** One slip has become a life sentence. Would you say that to a friend?
- **"I've ruined everything, so I may as well carry on."** Chapter 28 called this the second one, and it's the only truly dangerous thought on the list.
- **"From now on I must be perfect: up at five, cold shower, an hour of prayer, no sugar."** Here guilt has dressed itself up as discipline. You'll keep it up for four days, collapse, and reach for comfort.
- **"Other men are on day two hundred and I can't manage twenty. I must be a hopeless case."** You're comparing yourself with a number on a stranger's screen. You don't know how he's doing, and it doesn't matter.
- **"I shouldn't even feel desire."** Yes, you should. Desire is God's idea, as Chapter 3 said. You're a man and not a statue. Noticing that a woman is beautiful is not a fall. The sin was never the noticing. It was the taking.

Every one of those thoughts feels like repentance, and none of them is. Repentance is quick and it faces forward: confess, get up, find the instruction you broke. The prophet Micah speaks for a man in exactly this spot: "Don't rejoice against me, my enemy. When I fall, I will arise."

### Wanting it to hurt {-}

Religious men get one snare all to themselves.

A man follows this method and finds stopping easy. Then he feels guilty that it was easy. Surely, after all those years, it ought to cost something. Surely he should suffer a little, by way of payment. So some part of him sets about making it hard: brooding, punishing himself, even half welcoming a fall so that he can feel properly wretched afterwards.

See that for what it is. It's the Little Monster in a hair shirt. If you're a Christian you know perfectly well who paid, and it wasn't you. Trying to add your own suffering to the bill isn't humility. The debt was cleared in full. You don't owe misery on top, so take the freedom and be glad of it.

### The bully {-}

Keep the Little Monster separate from yourself. He isn't you. He's something that got attached to you when you were a boy.

Think of the playground bully throwing a tantrum for your lunch money. What happens if you pay him? He comes back tomorrow, louder. What happens if you don't? He blusters, he threatens, and then he slopes off. You can't argue him out of it and you needn't fight him. You simply don't pay.

A slip means you paid him once. You have no reason to open an account. Pick yourself up, work out where you let your guard down, and go back to enjoying being free.

### The men who quit the pebble {-}

If a slip has left you taking the whole business very solemnly, here's some medicine. EasyPeasy borrows a parody from a writer called Guillaco, who imagined a support forum for people trying to give up drinking bleach. I've stolen the idea and changed the poison. Meet the brave men of a forum I've made up, who are trying to stop walking around with a sharp pebble in their shoe.

"Day 19 pebble-free. Walked past a gravel drive this morning and nearly lost it. Stay strong, brothers."

"I allow myself the pebble on Sundays only. I think that's a healthy balance."

"Honestly, how is a man supposed to stop? I've always got feet. I've always got shoes. The temptation is with me every waking hour."

"I was doing so well. Then I had a stressful week at work and before I knew it I was in the garden, picking one out. A small one. I'm so ashamed. Resetting my counter."

"Does anyone else find the limp sort of comforting?"

"My accountability partner checks my shoes every Friday. So far so good, though I did think about the beach all through the sermon."

You're smiling because you can see what they can't. Nobody needs courage, a counter or a Friday inspection to keep a pebble out of his shoe. All he needs is to notice that it hurts and that it never did a thing for him. Once he's seen that, leaving it out isn't an achievement. It's just walking.

How many times this week were you tempted to put a stone in your shoe? None. That isn't self-control. You see a stone for what it is.

If you slipped, the lesson is not "try harder". Somewhere you started believing again that the pebble had something to offer. Find where, go back to that chapter, and read it again. Reading this book a second time is no disgrace and takes only a few hours. The world repeats its lies daily, so it does no harm to hear the truth twice.

## What about porn? What about sex? {-}

Two short answers.

**Porn.** It goes with the rest. I don't mean afterwards and I don't mean gradually. It's the same trap with a screen attached, and the two feed each other, as the man in the Introduction found out twice. Everything in this book applies to it. If you want more on porn alone, read [EasyPeasy](https://easypeasymethod.org/) as well. It is free, and this book grew out of it.

**Sex.** This book has nothing against sex. It's against a counterfeit of it. Within marriage, sex is a gift, and Chapter 21 told the married man not to hold back from his wife. If you're single, the answer isn't to go looking for somebody to use in place of your hand. That's the same lust, only now there's a victim. Chapter 21 also made the "try it and see" suggestion about noticing what happens to your energy. That offer stands, and it's all I'll promise on the subject.

## Where this book leaves EasyPeasy's path {-}

In one place we part company with our parent on purpose, and you should know it.

EasyPeasy, following Allen Carr, ends with a last deliberate session, entered with eyes open, to fix in the mind how little there is in it. Many people have found that useful for porn and for cigarettes. We don't do it. Our final step was the prayer in Chapter 27. Nobody takes leave of a sin by committing it carefully.

Nor do you need to. If you carried on as normal while reading, you've had dozens of sessions with your eyes open already. You may have been free for a while before you found this book. If so, don't go back to feed the Little Monster for the sake of a ceremony. He'd only start nagging again.

## Help end the silence {-}

The scandal with this habit isn't an industry. Nobody needs to sell it, since every boy is born with the equipment. What's scandalous is that nobody talks.

Look at the two messages a boy receives. The world tells him cheerfully that it's healthy, normal, even good for him, and asks no further questions. The church, for the most part, tells him nothing at all. Or it mentions it once at a youth weekend, in a tone that guarantees he'll never raise it again. Between the shrug and the silence he's left to work it out for himself at thirteen. He works it out wrong, as we all did.

Human beings got as far as we have because one generation tells the next where the pits are. Even a sparrow warns its young about the cat. But on this subject, the commonest private struggle among men, fathers who were caught for twenty years say not one word to their sons. They aren't cruel. They're ashamed, and so the trap gets handed down like a family heirloom.

Scare campaigns won't fix it. They never have. Frighten a boy and he'll do it frightened. Frighten a man and you've handed him one more bad feeling to escape from.

What fixes it is someone speaking plainly and kindly, which you're now able to do.

You'll remember the story Jesus told about a man who was beaten and left by the roadside. Two respectable religious people saw him, crossed over, and walked by on the far side. They didn't wish him harm. They were only embarrassed, busy, and unsure what to say. The one who stopped was the last person anyone expected.

Most of us have been walking past each other for years. Every man on the road is carrying the same wound, and every one of them looks straight ahead.

So I'd ask you to stop for one. You don't have to become a campaigner. But when you see a man grinding through a streak on willpower, point him here. When a friend makes the usual joke, you might just say, "I gave that up, actually. Best thing I've done." And when your son reaches the age, talk to him.

Now and then you'll get a blank look or a laugh. More often than you'd think, you'll get a message a week later that begins, "Can I ask you something?"

## Final warning {-}

You are a free man, and the years ahead of you are good ones. To keep them that way, hold on to these few things. Mark this page and come back whenever you like.

1. **If you ever catch yourself envying a man who still does it, remember he'd swap with you tonight.** He's the one going without. You aren't.
2. **You didn't enjoy the habit. That's why you left it.** What you enjoy is being free of it.
3. **"Just once" doesn't exist.** One is the first of a chain.
4. **Never reopen your decision.** You made it with a clear head, and it was right. It will still be right on your worst day.
5. **If you're in real difficulty, get help from a person.** That might be your pastor, a Christian counsellor, or a doctor. The Appendix has more. Asking is what a free man does, and nobody should be ashamed of it.
